However, being able to always provide the extra functionality of `IDataSourceAwareMetadataDomainRepository`, given any `IMetadataDomainRepository`, while possible, will not be as efficient because the data source type would need to be discovered everytime, using the old, slow method (by calling `getDomain(.)` and parsing the domain file). Concluding, with this solution, the slow and fast implementations would both need to exist and be maintained separately.

Another solution would be to subclass `SessionCachingMetadataDomainRepository` and define a new `DataSourceTypeAwareSessionCachingMetadataDomainRepository` class which would implement `IDataSourceAwareMetadataDomainRepository` and would require being given a `IDataSourceAwareMetadataDomainRepository` delegate. The Principals on the Subject interface is supposed to provide the principals of the Subject (the person logged in).   """"**Principals simply bind names to a Subject**"""" (as stated by the JAAS specification of [Subject](https://docs.oracle.com/javase/9/docs/api/javax/security/auth/Subject.html)).  This should be a Set containing the User identification (by name), including roles (by name) or groups (by name) in which the user can operate or belongs to.

For Waffle, these roles are supposed to be (according to documentation) the Windows groups to which the subject (user or computer) belongs.  In this case the """"name"""" used is either the FQN or the SID of the user and/or Windows security group.  The Principals returned by the WindowsLoginModule should therefore be of type (interface) Principal, for which getName should return a name of the user or a name of a Windows group to which the user belongs.
The line of code which was deleted by the breaking change and which I have put back, is the line that places the Windows Groups (names) as """"roles"""" in the Subject's Principals list.

The existing code for WindowsLoginModule (since October 2016) does not bind the Windows (or Active DIrectory) group (names) to the Subject.  It binds an object named """"Roles"""" to the Subject.  It therefore does not fulfill the basic function required of a JAAS WindowsLoginModule.

The packaging into a GroupPrincipal (which did not exist before the breaking change), was made to get it to work with WildFly (earlier versions as it does not work with latest versions in any case).  Every Windows Group to which the User belongs, was placed into a new list of Principals (named """"Roles"""") which was then packaged as a Principal (the GroupPrincipal) and added to the Subject.Principals list.  This is just plain **wrong**, as it assumes that any user of the subject will know about the custom """"Roles"""", and be able to extract the Principals from this list,    This assumption is obviously invalid.  The JAAS specified way is to obtain it from the Subject.Principles.getName(). The code modification also removed the ability to obtain the Windows Group (or JAAS roles) from the Subject.Principles.getName() as specified by JAAS.

The only reason I left the """"duplication"""" code in there (including the definition of a GroupPrincipal), is because I do not know who is dependent on this incorrect implementation. column2: DR**: We should only process `@AutoValueMapper` annotations observed on the return types of activity effect models, not all such annotations. If we want to extend `@AutoValueMapper` to non-activity-input/output cases, we can deploy another scoping mechanism (or lean on an existing one). While `@AutoValueMapper` should not be """"owned"""" by activity type processing, it's not a wholly independent process, either.)

column1: Looking ahead to a better-behaved processor, this approach of generating a single mapper family for all `@AutoValueMapper`s observed in the first round (and thus ignoring / failing on later rounds) probably isn't tenable in the long term. I don't think we need to change that behavior but we *should* think about what kind of annotation design will allow us to do better in the future with a minimum of churn for customers.
As I understand it, the value of `@AutoValueMapper` comes in two parts:
* The generation of a `ValueMapper` implementation for each annotated type.
* The generation of a mapper family with a factory method for each `ValueMapper` generated above.
The first part is easy to do incrementally, since each mapper implementation is independent of the others.

The second is not so easy, because we can only generate the mapper family once we know about all of the mappers it needs to reference. If we just go off of the list returned by `roundEnv.getElementsAnnotatedWith()` in one round, then we will miss any `@AutoValueMapper`-annotated elements generated in later rounds. There are basically three ways to handle this kind of aggregate output:

1. Don't output the mapper family until the final round. This lets us accumulate all `@AutoValueMapper` requests until the last possible moment, but other annotation processors won't be able to process the resulting mapper family. This may be an acceptable solution for some kinds of output that aren't meant to be processed further.

2. Limit the scope of `@AutoValueMapper`s considered, so that we can enumerate a full list early in the process and thus know exactly when there are no further mappers to consider. This is exactly what `@WithActivityType` does for activity types
column2: we provide a courtesy check that all `@ActivityType`-annotated elements are claimed by a `@WithActivityType`, but morally, we're only processing activity types referenced from the `package-info.java` annotations. We can do this explicitly (e.g. `@WithAutoMapperFor(...)`) or implicitly (""""all and only `@AutoValueMapper`s on return values from an activity type's effect model), but we must ultimately circumscribe some closed family of elements that we actually process.

column1: 3. For each `@AutoValueMapper`, generate a mapper family with one factory method, rather than accumulating all of them into a single family. We still need some way to know when we have a full set of `TypeRule`s, which implies that a user would have to add an `@WithMappers` for every single output type.

You might think we could get away with (1) here, because we don't actually need to process the generated mapper family since we're generating its `TypeRule`s ahead of time. Unfortunately, we have a similar problem, in that we don't want to resolve mappers for types until we have all of the `TypeRule`s available. If we started resolving without all of the rules, we might end up using an implementation we wouldn't have. As a very concrete example, we currently have a catch-all rule for any enum. If an activity returns an enum annotated with `@AutoValueMapper` (ignoring that it's currently built only for records, I hope we see that this is a splinter of the full story of use), then we might accidentally use the catch-all rather than the specific enum mapper. What a hard problem to debug!

I also think (3) is a non-starter, because it basically requires a user to add both a `@WithMappers` and a `@WithActivityType` for each activity type. This seems redundant, and also easy to forget about when developing an activity type (e.g. changing its return from `void` to an actual output).

On the other hand, I think (2) is pretty tenable. `@AutoValueMapper` would not be processed in the absence of other information (because we run into the open family issue again), but rather describes an inert desire *in the scope of* some other process. We can generate an `ActivityAttributeMappers` class covering all *and only* the value mappers for the processed activity types, which is a closed family because the activity types are themselves a closed family (enumerated by `@WithActivityTypes`.""",factory,Yes,comentarios_classificados_pt10_2a_exec.csv,NO_ARCHITECTURAL_TEST_POSSIBLE,TRUE,TRUE,0,0,"The generated test `NO_ARCHITECTURAL_TEST_POSSIBLE` is syntactically valid and correctly uses ArchUnit by not attempting an invalid test, but it does not represent the rule at all. First, the model we care about primarily is our data model (the entities). That drives how we store data and how we work with data at the logic level. The DTOs and various DTO-like things (adapter \*Info interfaces) are views into that model or data. We try to keep them as a subset of the data layer, but that isn't always possible due to preexisting conditions, usages, or just some legacy behavior we cannot remove or update for some reason. In any event, the data model is what drives most of the design of everything around it, not the views.

In the case of the adapter interfaces, they are a stopgap implementation to get adapter consumers (IT) to stop using our internal model objects and start using their own, for both maintenance and performance reasons. However, as soon as the adapter's model changed, we had to address the fallout of how the adapters were designed and intended to be used vs how they ended up actually being used
column2: coupled with the fact we now had code that was reliant on multiple versions of the model (data, manifest view and adapter view). So, we were left with a few options, one of which was rewrite every bit of code that surrounded the adapters (i.e. most of the manifest processing, chunks of refresh, etc.), which, as I'm sure you can imagine, was deemed unviable given the sheer volume of such work. After several discussions we landed on the interface + existing DTO reuse we have today. @kahowell might remember and have more to add here if he cares enough.

column1: Now, should the adapters have their own DTO implementations that we use? Maybe. Given how we seem to *want* to use the adapters, probably not, though. Well, the problem is that the token types from the jdt.ls will coexist with token types from other language servers. As a theme author, you won't necessarily know what language you're styling the tokens for (that's why LSP defines """"standard"""", generic token types). So someone who doesn't know about Java modules might see that the token type `module` is available, and style it based on the expectation that it has the same meaning as `namespace`. By prefixing it with `java`, it becomes clear that this is a Java-specific concept, and is semantically different from, let's say, modules in Rust. I don't think it matters *that much* in this particular case, but out of principle I made the decision to prefix it. Here's a quote from aeschli about this from [an earlier discussion](https://github.com/microsoft/vscode/issues/103097#issuecomment-672001256):

> If a custom token type or modifier is very language specific, it makes sense to prefix it that way: `javaMember` (extends member). But I don't think `javaMember` is a good example of a very 'java' specific concept.

This is also how the C# extension handles many language-specific token types, see [their `semanticTokenTypes` contribution](https://github.com/OmniSharp/omnisharp-vscode/blob/c09bf3f65319cc98fbf37f0070b9786ca4b16357/package.json#L3317-L3470). Additionally, [they even declare a `module` token type](https://github.com/OmniSharp/omnisharp-vscode/blob/c09bf3f65319cc98fbf37f0070b9786ca4b16357/package.json#L3415), which could potentially cause confusion with Java modules if they were not named `javaModule`. Although since the token type has no description I'm not entirely sure what it's used for anyway, especially since I'm no C# expert.

> After thinking for a while, or we can directly re-use `namespace` for modules. I don't see any case in Java to distinguish packages and modules, as they don't occur in the same file... both are some kind of `namespace`.

They *can* appear in the same file, since there are directives in module-info which refer to both module names and package names. Just see the test case for modules and you'll see what I mean. Personally I might style packages and modules the same, but they are semantically different and I don't like the idea of taking away customization abilities from theme authors without good reason.

When I put the logic in the getters, I found that computing the values on the fly after the request object was returned by the deserializer creates unexpected interactions between object attributes that would surprise developers at best and create hard-to-find bugs at worst. I chose the converter approach because it guarantees that the request object is fully """"baked"""" after the deserializer returns the object, and there would be no surprises to developers downstream. When I put the logic in the getters, I ended up with code like this (in `AwsProxyRequest.java`):

So the values of the multi-valued fields are not actually """"baked"""" when the `AwsProxyRequest` object is returned from the deserializer. Rather, the value of the multi-valued fields depend on the values of their respective single-valued fields, and the multi values are computed at the time of the first call to their getters when the single-valued field is also populated. If no multi values are included in the JSON being deserialized, then these call sequences on the request object returned from deserialization end up with different values in the multi-valued fields:
// multiValueQueryStringParameters is {""""foo"""": [""""bar""""]} at end of code block
// multiValueQueryStringParameters is {""""alpha"""": [""""bravo""""]} at end of code block
I thought that violated the principle of least surprise. No one would expect assignments to one field to affect the values retrieved from another field, and rightfully so.
You could avoid this by recomputing the multi-valued fields on every call to the getter (as opposed to storing it in the instance field), like this:
But now we're doing more (potentially a lot more) allocations and computations in getters, which isn't great either.

We could assign the multi-valued fields in the setter for the single-valued fields, but now we're potentially clobbering expected values in the multi-valued fields, and the ordering of calls to the single- and multi-valued fields could become unexpectedly significant.

We could also potentially work around the issue by tracking when each field is assigned with a separate flag variable, but that would make the order in which getters and setters are called significant, and JSON keys are unordered, by definition.

In my opinion, the core problem is that the request object's attributes are not """"baked"""" after the object is returned from the deserializer. What we really want is to run code to initialize the multi-valued fields one time before the deserialized object is returned to users. That is exactly what a Jackson converter does. By using the converter, we eliminate interactions between different attributes, and the request is now a POJO with no surprising behavior.

I readily acknowledge that I could be splitting hairs here that don't need splitting. If we embed the logic in the getters, then the """"bug"""" only reveals itself in very specific circumstances which may not be likely to happen in practice. But in my opinion, for whatever that's worth, it's better to avoid the bug, even if it leads to marginally less obvious code. (I agree that we need comments, though!) [Approach 1] is what you suggest, letting factory know what all instances of `TaxCalculator`s are available on compile time (Ether holding static map or writing a big switch case construct inside factory.) and having hard dependancy between implementations and factory.
[Approach 2] is registering all instances of `TaxCalculator` instances on deploy/bootstrap time, and letting factory only serve these instances on request.

The pros/cons of these approaches will not be apparent when number of implementations is very small (which is true in this case). However once your application starts growing and number of implementations increase, it will be hard to manage these instances statically inside factory.

That is where the [Approach 2] shines. Basically """"Single Responsibility"""" of `factory` here is only to serve instances and not to know what instances it is serving. In this case I added this logic to `Client` class since this is where all logic of bootstrapping resides, however I could have created a `TaxCalculatorFactoryConfiguration` class, and put this logic there.
This way the implementations can be registered agnostically on boot time (through dependency injection) and factory doesn't need to change when you add or remove implementations.

column1: re: Allowing an executable for the coverage dependency:

First, to make sure we're on the same page, when I say """"binary"""" I mean a top-level executable problem. I don't mean e.g. a shared library. I say this because something I've seen in OSS+Bazel+Python is, e.g. using `cc_binary` to produce a Python-loadable shared-library, and I've seen more C-centric people call them a binary.

Second, the way I see things, when we build e.g. a `py_binary`, things like the Python interpreter/runtime and coverage are inputs to that binary. This is because, essentially, that's how binary rules in Bazel are implemented: the binary rule gathers pieces from the toolchain, dependencies, etc and puts it all together into a final executable. But also because binaries, as the top-level entry point, should get the final say in how they work. (To be fair, I probably have some bias because, within Google, we use embedded Python, so Python is more a library used within a C program than separate runtime).

This is distinct from another way of thinking of things: that the `py_binary` and coverage are inputs to the Python interpreter (or that the py binary and interpreter are inputs to the coverage tool). This is more conceptually how non-Bazel Python works (you install a Python runtime, the add stuff into that runtime).

Insofar as Bazel is concerned, mixing together executables is problematic. In this case, we're mixing together a coverage executable and the py_binary executable. There are several ways this can interact badly, but it all comes down to each target specifying something that is mutually exclusive with something else. Examples include:
* Specifying different malloc implementations (in Google, we allow `py_binary` to specify a malloc implementation)
* Specifying or having different versions of the same the same library
* Having dependencies that are mutually exclusive (e.g. I think boringssl/openssl are mutually exclusive
column2: internally we have other such cases).

We saw this sort of issue internally very frequently when doing our Python 2 to 3 transition (a python 2 binary in the dependencies of a Python 3 binary, or vice versa, would fubar the build).
A couple other problems also occur when a binary is added to the dependencies (i.e. `deps` or equiv

column1: Using `py_binary` as an example again, recall that it (currently) has two outputs: the executable stub script and main .py file. We actually don't care about that executable stub script in this case, but it still has to be built and included into the runfiles (we're merging in its runfiles, as we must). If we built for e.g. windows, then we might get a `.exe` launcher that is entirely unused. In today's rules, this isn't too much overhead (the stub script is small), so nobody really notices. With something like embedded Python (or e.g. pyoxider etc), that overhead is pretty large.

This also segues into the next issue: the inner binary respects the flag settings intended for the outer binary. This is because it's being built in the same configuration (target, as it must). Going back to `py_binary`, if you specified, I think its the `--build_zip` flag (sp), then the inner binary would also build a (largely self-contained) zip file and use that as its output instead of e.g. the typical stub script. This isn't uncommon for binaries. While libraries can also have flags, it's not really an issue -- they still abide by the """"I'm a thing to be included in another thing"""" contract.

I use `py_binary` as a convenient, if presently impossible, example.
